verses.translation_literal: A song, a psalm, of Asaph.
verses.translation_dramatic: A song. A psalm of Asaph, for the singers to carry.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the only verse of the psalm that is not spoken to God, and it is the label on the scroll. The Hebrew counts it as verse 1, which is why every verse of this psalm is numbered one higher than in the KJV, whose 83:0 leaves it unnumbered. 'Song' and 'psalm' are two terms side by side: shir is the sung piece, mizmor a piece accompanied by strings (from zamar, 'to pluck'). Asaph was David's Levite choirmaster, and the Asaph guild kept singing under his name for centuries, so 'of Asaph' tells the actors this was a temple liturgy, sung by a crowd, not a private complaint. Radak, Meiri and Malbim tie it to Jehoshaphat's war in 2 Chronicles 20, where a descendant of Asaph, Jahaziel, speaks. The Targum calls it 'a song and praise by the hand of Asaph'.

philological_notes.note: A psalm: a song sung with instrumental accompaniment; the noun appears in 57 psalm titles.
The preposition lamed can mean 'by', 'for' or 'belonging to the guild of'; the commentators read it as the Levite family that sang before the ark.

verses.translation_literal: God, let there be no silence for you; do not be mute, and do not be still, O God.
verses.translation_dramatic: God, do not hold your silence. Do not be mute, do not be still. Speak, O God, and let the quiet end.
verses.directors_commentary: Open on a plea, not a greeting. Three words for silence pile up in one breath: domi (stillness, a hush), heresh (to be mute, even deaf, the opposite of answering) and shaqat (to be at rest, to do nothing). Malbim splits them well: not to answer, and not to act. Play it as a crowd that has waited too long and cannot stand the quiet. The KJV renders the first as 'keep not thou silence' and the other two as 'hold not thy peace' and 'be not still', which is faithful but makes them sound like three ways of saying one thing; the Hebrew makes the silence heavier each time. The double address, 'God' (Elohim) at the start and 'God' ('El) at the end, frames the verse like a hand held out and not taken. Rashi hears a request not to give silence to the enemies' noise, whose roar is about to be described.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'no stillness to you'; an unusual construction with a noun, not a verb, as a prayer. Ibn Ezra links it to 'and Aaron was silent' (Lev 10:3) while noting it is another root.
To be mute or deaf; Malbim says it is the opposite of answering, whereas 'be still' (shaqat) is the opposite of acting.

verses.translation_literal: For behold, your enemies roar, and those who hate you have lifted [the] head.
verses.translation_dramatic: For listen: your enemies are roaring like a sea in storm, and those who hate you have lifted their heads high.
verses.directors_commentary: 'Behold' (hinneh) points the audience's finger at the noise outside. The verb yehemayun is the sound of a crowd, a stormy sea or a growling animal; the same root is used for a city in uproar. Ibn Ezra connects it to hamon, 'multitude': the roar is their numbers. The KJV 'make a tumult' is accurate but flat. 'Lifted the head' is an idiom of arrogance in battle: you raise your head when you no longer fear. The enemies are God's enemies, not Israel's, which is the argument of the whole psalm: the people appeal that the quarrel is God's own. Note the shift from the plea to the report, which the actors should give a sharp turn of the head.

philological_notes.note: To growl, moan, roar; used of crowds, seas and doves. The long ending -un is archaic and poetic.
'Lifted the head': an idiom of confidence and insolence. Metzudat David reads it as rising ever higher.

verses.translation_literal: Against your people they make crafty [their] counsel, and they take counsel together against your treasured ones.
verses.translation_dramatic: Against your people they spin their secret plans, cunning and low; they put their heads together against those you keep hidden and prize.
verses.directors_commentary: The noise of verse 3 turns into whispering. Sod is the circle of confidants, the council behind closed doors, and ya'arimu is the verb of the serpent in Eden (arum, 'shrewd'): the nations are not boiling with rage, they are being clever. The KJV 'taken crafty counsel' is right, and its 'hidden ones' keeps a good double sense: tsefunekha are those God has 'hidden' as a treasure, or sheltered. The BBE's 'those whom you keep in a secret place' takes only the first sense. Radak reads them as Israel, tucked under God's shelter. Malbim goes further: they plot against God's hidden things, his oneness and his law. Play the contrast: their secret plots against the people God himself has secreted away.

philological_notes.note: 'Make counsel crafty': to plan shrewdly in secret. Ibn Ezra glosses it 'crafty secret'; sod can mean both a council and its secret.
'Your hidden/treasured ones': what is stored away and protected. Radak reads it as Israel hidden in God's shelter.

verses.translation_literal: They have said, "Go! and let us wipe them out from [being] a nation, and the name of Israel will not be remembered any more."
verses.translation_dramatic: They have said it aloud: "Come, let us wipe them out, till they are a nation no more, till no one remembers the name of Israel."
verses.directors_commentary: The first quoted speech of the enemies, and it is a plan of erasure, not conquest. Nakhchidem is from kachad, 'to hide, conceal', used in the causative for 'wipe out' (Exod 23:23); the KJV's 'cut them off' is a fair paraphrase but misses that it means to make them vanish. In the ancient Near East a name that is no longer spoken is a people that never was, which is why the threat is aimed at 'the name of Israel'. Rashi (on the next verse) takes the stake higher: God is called God of Israel, so once Israel's name is no longer remembered, God's great name is no longer remembered either. Malbim adds that 'Israel' is the name of a people led above the course of nature and watched over by the LORD, so to cancel the name is to cancel that claim. 'Come' is lekhu, literally 'go', the ordinary imperative of urging ('Come, let us...'), as when Joseph's brothers say lekhu ve-nahargehu, 'Come, let us kill him' (Gen 37:20). The Hebrew has no quotation marks; the actors should hear this as the enemies' own cry.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of kachad, 'to hide'; in the causative, 'to destroy, wipe out'. Metzudat Zion compares 'and you shall be destroyed from the earth' (Exod 9).
'From being a nation' (Ibn Ezra, Radak): the aim is to strip them of nationhood, not necessarily of life.
Plural imperative of halakh, 'go', used as 'come on, let us': the call to join in a plan. Gen 37:20 has the same form before a cohortative.

token_glosses.gloss: and let us wipe them out

verses.translation_literal: For they have taken counsel [with one] heart together; against you they cut a covenant.
verses.translation_dramatic: For they have taken counsel with a single heart, and against you, against you, they cut a covenant.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the hinge of the psalm. 'Against your people' becomes 'against you': the alliance is aimed at God. 'Cut a covenant' is the Hebrew idiom for making a treaty, since a treaty was sealed by cutting animals in two and walking between the halves; the KJV 'confederate' loses the blood in the image. The irony is deliberate: the covenant (berit) is the word Israel uses for its bond with God, and here the nations make a counter-covenant. 'One heart' (lev yachdav) is a unity of mind; Radak and Malbim stress that peoples who were fighting each other have made peace to fight Israel. The 'for' (ki) explains why God must speak: the stakes are not Israel's survival but his name, as Rashi says. The ASV 'with one consent' is a good idiom but turns 'heart' into 'consent'.

philological_notes.note: 'They cut a covenant': a treaty sealed by cutting. The imperfect shows the act in progress.
Niphal of ya'ats, 'to take counsel together'; 'heart' is the accusative of respect, 'in heart', i.e. 'with one mind'.

verses.translation_literal: The tents of Edom and the Ishmaelites; Moab and the Hagrites;
verses.translation_dramatic: The tents of Edom, and the sons of Ishmael; Moab, and the Hagrites;
verses.directors_commentary: A roll call. Read it slowly, as names called at a gate: ten nations in three verses, almost all of them neighbours who share Abraham, Isaac or Lot as ancestors; the cousins of Israel are the first to come. 'Tents of Edom' is the unusual start: the KJV 'tabernacles' is archaic, and the Hebrew ohel means the plain nomad's tent, not a sacred one. Ibn Ezra reads the tents as a sign of the nomadic way of life. The Ishmaelites are the descendants of Hagar's son and the Hagrites are a related tribe east of the Jordan (1 Chr 5:10, 19-20); Radak and Metzudat David derive the latter from Hagar by another father. The KJV 'Hagarenes' is a Latinized form. The listing is probably not one campaign but the psalmist's survey of all the hostile peoples around.

philological_notes.note: 'Tents of Edom': a figure for the people as tent-dwellers; Ibn Ezra reads it as the Edomites who live in tents or the tents that joined them.
The Hagrites, a tribe named after Hagar; Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David say the sons of Hagar by another husband, not Abraham.

verses.translation_literal: Gebal and Ammon and Amalek; Philistia with the inhabitants of Tyre;
verses.translation_dramatic: Gebal, and Ammon, and Amalek; Philistia, with the people of Tyre;
verses.directors_commentary: The roll call widens from the desert to the coast. Gebal is probably the Phoenician port Byblos, though some commentators place it near Edom (Ibn Ezra: 'the Gebalites'); Tyre is the great Phoenician trading city. Amalek is the first enemy Israel met after the exodus, and the Torah vows God's war against it forever (Exod 17:16). Philistia is the coastal enemy of the judges and of David. So the circle runs south, east, north and west: no border is safe. The KJV 'the Philistines' turns the land (Peleshet) into the people. The list is deliberately all-surrounding; the actors should let the list run on, with growing breathlessness.

philological_notes.note: Gebal: Phoenician Byblos in the usual reading; Ibn Ezra, Radak and the Targum read 'Gebalites', a people.

verses.translation_literal: Also Asshur has joined himself with them; they have become an arm for the sons of Lot. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: Even Assyria has joined them. They have become the strong arm of the sons of Lot. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: Assyria, the farthest and the greatest, comes last, and the word 'also' (gam) marks the surprise. The Hebrew form 'Asshur' is the old name; the KJV's 'Assur' is a transliteration, and 'holpen' is archaic for 'helped'. 'They have become an arm' (zero'a) is a figure of military strength: Assyria is the muscle, and the sons of Lot, Moab and Ammon, are the body. Rashi and Radak read the surprise morally: Assyria had stayed apart from the evil counsel (Gen 10:11), or had forgotten the angel that struck its camp. The Targum names Sennacherib. Selah marks a pause, of uncertain meaning, perhaps a musical interlude; hold the silence before the next verse. It also turns the psalm: the list ends, the plea returns.

philological_notes.note: Niphal of lavah, 'to join oneself to, to attach'; Metzudat Zion compares 'this time my husband will be joined to me' (Gen 29:34).
'Arm': the strength of a nation in war; here a helper, an auxiliary force.
A term of uncertain meaning, probably a pause or musical sign; left untranslated in the literal layer.

verses.translation_literal: Do to them as to Midian, as to Sisera, as to Jabin, at the wadi of Kishon.
verses.translation_dramatic: Do to them as you did to Midian; as to Sisera, as to Jabin, at the wadi of Kishon.
verses.directors_commentary: Now the psalm turns from the enemies' roar to God's own old victories, and it asks for repetition. The imperative asei (do) is short and hard, a command to the divine warrior. Midian is Gideon's victory (Judges 7), Sisera and Jabin the victory of Deborah and Barak (Judges 4-5); in both God, not the army, won, which is why the psalmist chooses them. The KJV's 'brook of Kison' is the same wadi: a seasonal watercourse in the Jezreel plain that flooded with rain and swept away Sisera's chariots (Judg 5:21). Ibn Ezra and Meiri quote that line, 'the wadi Kishon swept them away'. A modern audience should hear 'wadi' as a dry streambed that a storm can turn into a torrent in an hour. Note the compressed rhythm: three 'as'-phrases in a row, like three blows.

philological_notes.note: A wadi, a seasonal stream; Judges 5:21 says it swept Sisera's army away.

verses.translation_literal: They were destroyed at En-dor; they became dung for the ground.
verses.translation_dramatic: They were destroyed at En-dor; they lay there, dung for the ground.
verses.directors_commentary: The image is meant to be ugly. Domen is manure, spread on a field, the commonest thing underfoot; the KJV 'dung' is correct, but the BBE's 'dust and waste' softens it. The corpses of the enemy are fertilizer, with no burial and no name, the exact reverse of the 'name remembered' they wanted for themselves in verse 5. 'En-dor' (Spring of Dor) lay in Manasseh's territory near Tabor and Megiddo (Josh 17:11), but the book of Judges names no battle there, and the commentators differ on which one the psalm means. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat David take it back to Midian, Gideon's victory, though Radak admits Judges does not say so; Radak also records others who refer it to Sisera. Meiri and Malbim apply it to Jabin and Sisera, whose Canaanite power reached En-dor and who fled there before Barak, since Deborah's song places the kings of Canaan at Taanach by the waters of Megiddo. Rashi says plainly that he does not know which war it was. Say the line quietly and flatly, with no triumph, as a fact.

philological_notes.note: Dung, manure heap; used of corpses in 2 Kings 9:37 and Jeremiah 8:2. Radak and Metzudat David say the corpses were trampled like dung on the ground.

En-dor: 'spring of Dor' in the territory of Manasseh (Josh 17:11); Saul's medium later lived there (1 Sam 28). The battle the psalm means is disputed: Midian (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Metzudat David) or Jabin and Sisera (Meiri, Malbim); Rashi does not decide.

verses.translation_literal: Make them, their nobles, like Oreb and like Zeeb, and like Zebah and like Zalmunna, all their princes.
verses.translation_dramatic: Make their nobles like Oreb and like Zeeb, and all their princes like Zebah and Zalmunna.
verses.directors_commentary: Four Midianite leaders are named, and two of them are animal names: Oreb is 'raven' and Zeeb is 'wolf'. In Judges 7:25 Gideon's Ephraimites kill them at the rock of Oreb and the winepress of Zeeb, so the names became places, and the psalm calls them back. Zebah ('sacrifice') and Zalmunna ('shade denied', or 'protection withheld') were Midianite kings whom Gideon killed himself (Judg 8). The KJV 'Make their nobles like Oreb' is accurate but hides the beast names; the actors should feel the irony of a raven and a wolf, birds and beasts of prey, who became carrion. The Hebrew construction 'make them, their nobles' puts the pronoun before the noun, as in 'she saw him, the child' (Exod 2:6); Ibn Ezra and Radak say the same. 'Nobles' (nedivim) are the willing leaders and 'princes' (nesikhim) the ones appointed or anointed; the KJV flattens both to 'nobles' and 'princes' without that nuance.

philological_notes.note: 'Make them': the pronoun anticipates the noun 'their nobles'; Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri compare 'she saw him, the child' (Exod 2:6).
Oreb 'raven' and Zeeb 'wolf': the names of two Midianite chiefs killed by Ephraim (Judg 7:25).
'Their princes': Metzudat Zion links it with 'princes of Sihon' (Josh 13:21) as a term of rank.

verses.translation_literal: Who said: Let us take possession for ourselves of the pastures of God.
verses.translation_dramatic: These are the ones who said it, and said it aloud, with the hunger of a thief counting another man's flock: "Let it be ours. Let us take for ourselves the pastures of God."
verses.directors_commentary: The speakers are the coalition named in verses 7–9, and their boast is the whole reason for the prayer. Play it as a quotation: the psalmist repeats their words back to God as evidence. The verb "take possession" (yarash) is the covenant word for Israel's own settlement of the land, so the enemy is taking up Israel's vocabulary and aiming it at Israel. The KJV's "houses of God" is a harmonizing guess. The Hebrew ne'ot means pastures, grazing grounds, dwellings of shepherds. Rashi reads the "dwelling of God's house", that is the Temple; Radak and Meiri read the land of Israel; Metzudat David the place of the sanctuary. Either way God is a shepherd-landlord whose range is being claimed. A hearer from a pastoral society would feel the word as plain theft of grazing land. YLT's "comely places" takes the same consonants as the adjective "fitting, lovely"; it is possible, but the context of dispossession favors "pastures".

philological_notes.note: Construct plural of nawe/naweh, a pasture or the dwelling of shepherds, here God's own range. Ibn Ezra notes the letters א ה ו י interchange, so ne'ot stands for newot.
Cohortative 'let us take possession'; the verb of the conquest and inheritance of Canaan, turned here against its heirs.

verses.translation_literal: My God, set them like the tumbling thing, like chaff before wind.
verses.translation_dramatic: My God. Make them as the thistle-head that has no root, rolling over the dry ground; make them as chaff that cannot stand before the wind.
verses.directors_commentary: The voice turns from quoting the enemy to addressing God, and it turns personal: "my God" (Ibn Ezra notes that the possessive marks a single, intimate address after the plural "God" of the last verse). The images belong to the threshing floor and the summer hillside. Galgal, from the root "to roll", is a tumbling thing; Rashi and Radak take it as the dry head of a field thorn that breaks off in the autumn and rolls before the wind, and Isaiah 17:13 pairs it with the same wind. The KJV's "wheel" is a different guess from the same root and loses the plant. Chaff (qash) is what is thrown into the air at the winnowing and blown off the floor: weightless, worthless, and gone. Nothing here says the enemy is destroyed by sword; they are made light.

philological_notes.note: From 'to roll'; a rolling object blown by the wind. Rashi and Radak: a dried thorn head or stubble; Isaiah 17:13 has the same image. Versions split between 'wheel', 'whirling dust' and 'rolling thing'.
Chaff or dry stubble, the light waste of the threshing floor.

verses.translation_literal: Like fire it burns a forest, and like a flame it sets mountains ablaze,
verses.translation_dramatic: As fire takes a forest, tree leaning on tree until nothing is left standing; as flame runs up the mountainsides and sets the ridges alight.
verses.directors_commentary: The picture moves from small to vast: chaff, then a forest, then whole mountains. The sentence is unfinished; verse 16 supplies its "so". The two images are one: fire in the forest, flame on the hills. Radak and Metzudat David point to the trees standing close together, so that fire passes from one to the next, and to the wind on the heights that fans it; Malbim draws the human lesson, that the enemy's own ranks burn each other, which fits the tradition that these armies turned on one another (2 Chron 20:23). The two Hebrew verbs are nearly synonyms (ba'ar, lahat): the second is the rarer, poetic verb for a blaze that licks and consumes. The KJV renders it correctly in meaning; the Hebrew's rhythm of two fire words in two lines is what a reader should hear.

philological_notes.note: Piel, 'sets ablaze, makes flame'; the same root as 'flaming' in Psalm 104:4 and the blazing sword at Eden, Gen 3:24.

verses.translation_literal: So may you pursue them with your storm, and with your storm-wind may you terrify them.
verses.translation_dramatic: So drive them down. Hunt them with your tempest, and let your whirlwind close around them until terror is all they have left.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the "so" that completes the double simile: as fire and flame, so you. The verbs are imperfects used as a wish, and they mean what they say. Pursue (radaf) is a hunter's and a soldier's word, so the storm is pictured as a chasing army, and the enemy as quarry. Malbim separates the two winds: sa'ar blows in one direction and drives them off; sufah is the whirling wind that turns them back and so terrifies them. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion call both strong wind. The KJV's "persecute" is the old sense of pursue and now reads wrongly, as if the enemy were being harassed for belief; the word means chase. "Make them afraid" is a weak rendering of bahal, a word for sudden panic, the jolt of dismay. The audience knows a God who commands wind and storm.

philological_notes.note: Pursue, chase, as a hunter or an army does. The KJV 'persecute' preserves the old meaning 'pursue', which is now misleading.
A whirlwind or storm-wind; Malbim distinguishes it from sa'ar as a wind that circles from every side. Rashi glosses with an Old French word for a whirlwind.

verses.translation_literal: Fill their faces with shame, that they may seek your name, YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: Fill their faces with shame, until the burning of it shows in every cheek. And let them then seek your name, O LORD.
verses.directors_commentary: The prayer turns from wind to the face. "Fill their faces" is the physical language of shame: the face is where honor lives and where its loss is seen. Qalon, shame, is related by Radak's father and Metzudat Zion to the idea of being scorched, so that the face reddens as if roasted; others tie it to qal, light, as in making them light and contemptible. The reversal is deliberate: they set out to treat God's land as their prize (verse 13) and are given dishonor in place of the honor they hoped for (Ibn Ezra, Radak). The second half is a surprise. "That they may seek your name" is a purpose clause, and the Hebrew does not say whether the seeking is repentance or only recognition. The commentators split: Radak and Metzudat David read a genuine turning, Meiri applies it to Israel, Malbim says they seek too late. The KJV's "O Lord" for YHWH hides that the psalm now speaks the covenant name itself, the name the enemies are asked to seek.

philological_notes.note: Shame, dishonor. Medieval commentators connect it to qali, 'roasted' (a face burning with shame), or to qal, 'light'.
Jussive: 'and let them seek'. Whether it means repentance or only forced recognition is disputed.

verses.translation_literal: May they be ashamed and be terrified forever, and may they be abashed and perish.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let them be put to shame. Let terror hold them, now and always. Let them be abashed, and let them be lost.
verses.directors_commentary: The mood hardens. After the hopeful "seek your name" the psalm piles up four verbs of defeat: shame, terror, abashment, perishing. Bosh and hafer both mean to be ashamed (Radak glosses hafer as bosh; Metzudat Zion cites Isaiah 24:23, where the moon is abashed), so the verse is built on two near-synonyms for disgrace plus the terror of verse 16. The final verb is the plain one: oved, to perish. The KJV's "confounded" and "troubled" are archaic and blur this: confounded is ashamed, troubled is panicked. The phrase "forever" (adei ad) is a double: "until perpetuity", the biggest time-word in the language. Metzudat David notes that they will not be spared by seeking, which sets this verse against the hope of verse 17 and leaves both in tension for the actor.

philological_notes.note: To be ashamed or abashed (a different verb from 'dig', חפר). Radak: it means the same as bosh; Isaiah 24:23 'the moon will be abashed'.

verses.translation_literal: And may they know that you, your name is YHWH, you alone, Most High over all the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: And let them know, at the last, that you, whose name is the LORD, you and no other, are the Most High over all the earth.
verses.directors_commentary: The whole psalm has been asking for this: that the nations come to know who God is. The sentence is deliberately compressed; the Hebrew lays down "you", then "your name YHWH", then "alone", then "Most High". Ibn Ezra reads an omitted "who": you, whose name is YHWH. Radak and Metzudat David read that the name and the person are one, and that no one else holds the rule. The KJV's "whose name alone is Jehovah" attaches "alone" to the name, while the Hebrew word is "to your aloneness" and can attach to "you"; the ASV and BBE shift it to the person. Either reading says that YHWH is not one god among the ten gods of the coalition. "Most High" (Elyon) was an old title of God in Canaanite and Israelite religion; the psalm claims it for YHWH alone, and says his rule extends over all the earth, not only the land at stake in verse 13. The final word, erets, "earth" or "land", answers the land of the opening claim: the enemies wanted a piece of it; he owns all of it. The KJV prints "Jehovah" here, a form built on the vowels of Adonai that the Hebrew text does not have.

philological_notes.note: 'Most High', an old divine title. Malbim: it is a relative word, so the claim is that nothing exists above him; Radak: everything is under his hand.
'to your aloneness', that is 'you alone'. It may qualify 'you' or 'your name'; Ibn Ezra reads a missing 'who' and takes 'alone' with 'you'.
